items.title: Airstrikes on Iran Missile Sites May Shed Light on Justification for Dams
items.excerpt: Environmentalists have long puzzled over a wide network of water projects lacking any obvious justification. Then their areas were targeted in airstrikes.

items.title: Pope Endures Grueling Travel in South America Weeks After Surgery
items.excerpt: When doctors operated on Pope Leo XIV’s lung in October, some wondered if he’d postpone a long-planned trip to South America. It’s gone well so far.

items.title: Bahrain Convicts Dozens of Shiite Clerics in Sweeping Terrorism Trial
items.excerpt: The defendants were accused of colluding with Iran. Rights groups said the case was marred by torture allegations and raised concerns about religious persecution.

items.title: U.N. Starts Uncertain Effort to Regulate Lethal Autonomous Weapons
items.excerpt: Delegates met in Geneva to discuss guardrails for such systems even as their development grows. Russia and the United States have resisted the efforts.

items.title: Winter Nightmare Looms Early in Ukraine as Russia Strikes Relentlessly
items.excerpt: Even as it talks peace, Russia has opened a bombing campaign intended to strip Kyiv and other cities of heat, running water and sanitation this winter.

items.title: Trump’s Asia Trip Will Bring Him to the Table With Xi and Putin: What to Know
items.excerpt: President Trump will also meet with regional leaders, including Australia’s prime minister, who said “we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts.”

items.title: South Korea to Examine How K-Pop Industry Treats Underage Performers
items.excerpt: The announcement came after a New York Times investigation about the restrictive contracts of the group NewJeans, signed when its members were 14 to 17.

items.title: They Defeated a Strongman. But Can They Run a Country?
items.excerpt: Serbia’s student movement was deliberately leaderless and made group decisions to unseat Aleksandar Vucic. Now no one seems quite sure what happens next.

items.title: Searching for the Last Stoats of Waiheke Island
items.excerpt: Can the tourist destination become the first urban island to rid itself of the stoat — an introduced predator that has ravaged New Zealand’s endemic wildlife?

items.title: Canada’s Leader, Once a Curiosity at Asia Summits, Is Now a Star
items.excerpt: Prime Minister Mark Carney is courting Europe, but the bigger payoff might be in China, where he will share summit stages with Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and President Trump.

items.title: International Students Are Turning Away From U.S. Universities
items.excerpt: For a second year, Trump administration policies appear to be scaring away international students, disrupting the finances of the American colleges that depend on them.

items.title: Israel Kidnapped Iranian Generals in Hunt for Ron Arad
items.excerpt: Israeli officials were convinced that Tehran was to blame for the airman’s disappearance. Alternative theories got little attention, until now.

items.title: In Banff, a Grizzly Bear Known as ‘the Boss’ Rules the National Park
items.excerpt: Bear 122 has survived a train, cars and rival bears. Some fear the biggest threat to his life now is his own fame.

items.title: American Roosters Fight in the Philippines Despite U.S. Crackdown
items.excerpt: It’s illegal in the United States to transport game fowl for fighting. But investigators say breeders are sending birds to the Philippines, where cockfighting is legal and lucrative.

items.title: American Global Health Aid Isn’t Dead. It’s Changing.
items.excerpt: The Trump administration promised to make aid programs more “America First.” Some countries are balking.

items.title: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, Mexican Drug Lord, Dies in Prison
items.excerpt: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, who helped build the foundations of modern-day drug empires, was the subject of a major U.S. manhunt for his role in the murder of a D.E.A. agent.

items.title: Jordan Sentences 3 to Death Over Greek Orthodox Church Attack
items.excerpt: The Jordanian military said that the men, who were arrested after a shooting at a Greek Orthodox church last month, had been convicted of terrorism charges.

items.title: Too Many Chips in One Basket?
items.excerpt: The U.S. economy hitched its wagon to Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Now that he has stepped down, the company faces deep uncertainty.

items.title: Saudi-Backed Forces Retreat in Yemen, Leaving Key Strait in Houthi Control
items.excerpt: It’s a setback for the Yemeni government and its ally Saudi Arabia, as analysts said the momentum in country’s civil war was tilting toward the Iran-backed Houthis.

items.title: Iran Attacks Bahrain for the Second Time in Days
items.excerpt: The resumption of attacks after a two-month lull comes as peace talks between the U.S. and Iran appear to have stalled.

items.title: Is Italy the Model for Europe’s Future?
items.excerpt: Over more than a quarter-century, I’ve watched Europe’s politics become more like Italy’s, with all the resulting instability, as the far right came in from the cold.

items.title: In Europe, an Emboldened Iran Contributes to a Sense of Anxiety
items.excerpt: Prosecutors and government officials believe Iran or its proxies are behind a series of security breaches and threats in Britain and Europe, unsettling the region.

items.title: A Mexican Artist Sang Some of His Hits. Authorities Stopped the Show, Then Arrested Him.
items.excerpt: A concert by the singer Gabito Ballesteros was suspended after he sang songs that supposedly glorify cartel culture. The action has renewed a debate over culture and free speech.

items.title: South Sudan’s National Election, Its First, Will Be Delayed
items.excerpt: Analysts had warned that the vote, originally set for December, faced a legitimacy crisis. South Sudan has not held a national election since gaining independence in 2011.

items.title: Meet the Fans Who Traveled to Bangkok for Eurovision Asia
items.excerpt: Some were Asia-based Europeans chasing nostalgia. Others were Americans eager to experience their first edition of the song contest.

items.title: Asia’s Eurovision Contest Is Missing China, India, Pakistan, Indonesia and Japan
items.excerpt: China, India, Pakistan, Indonesia and Japan didn’t join the singing contest in Bangkok. That left some of the region’s best-known musical cultures out of the mix.

items.title: Asian love ballads test Eurovision’s winning song formula.
items.excerpt: While pulsating electro-pop tends to win in Europe, the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest in Asia will mostly feature torch songs accompanied by traditional instruments.

items.title: Geopolitics Looms Over Eurovision, but Not Its Asian Edition
items.excerpt: So far, the contest’s organizers have kept politics offstage. The European edition shows how difficult that can be.

items.title: Here’s the latest.
Ukraine’s Starshield Access Is Being Restricted Again, Zelensky Says
items.excerpt: President Volodymyr Zelensky said the system, which Ukraine uses to guide drones, was being throttled over Russian-occupied territory. SpaceX, its developer, has denied the claim.
